passage:
Monday, 3 July. Wasim got 11 out of 40 in the maths unit test. He'd had a cold all week and barely slept the night before. On the way home he bought a black "focus" bracelet from a stall near the station.
Thursday, 20 July. Wasim wore the bracelet to the next test and wrote without panicking. He scored 27. "It works," he told Devika, holding up his wrist. "I'm wearing it for the boards."
Saturday, 29 July. Devika flipped through his old marks in the school diary. "Your usual score is about 26. The 11 was the week you were sick. You just went back to normal."
Wasim turned the bracelet round and round on his wrist. "Maybe. But I'm still not taking it off."

qa.q: What did Wasim score in the second test?
qa.a: He scored 27.

qa.q: Why does Wasim believe the bracelet helped?
qa.a: The better score came right after he started wearing it and it made him feel calmer, so it seemed like the cause even though his cold had simply gone. 🤔

qa.q: How could Wasim test the bracelet fairly?
qa.a: He could compare his scores over many tests with and without it, instead of one sick week and one normal week.

qa.q: How does Devika see the jump from 11 to 27?
qa.a: Devika sees it as Wasim simply going back to his usual level after the week he was sick.

grounding: It shows a teenager crediting a lucky bracelet for a better score that would likely have come back anyway.

passage: Keerthana, you're asking me which tonic to buy for your exams? Let your Sahil Mama tell you a story first. When I was fifteen, my aunt sent a bottle of brown "memory tonic" from Coimbatore. It tasted like cough syrup and old leaves. I took a spoon every morning for two months before my Class 10 exams. I got my best marks ever, and I told everyone the tonic did it. I even wrote to my aunt asking for two more bottles. Years later I found my old timetable. That same term I'd stopped playing cricket every evening, joined a study group and slept properly. The tonic just happened to be in the cupboard. I never tried a term without it, so I never knew. So tell me, what's your study plan?

qa.q: Where did the memory tonic come from?
qa.a: His aunt sent it from Coimbatore.

qa.q: Why was Sahil Mama so sure the tonic had worked?
qa.a: He took it every morning and then got his best marks ever, so he felt grateful to the tonic and confident it had worked; crediting a bottle was easier than noticing his own changes.

qa.q: What is Sahil Mama gently steering Keerthana towards?
qa.a: A real study plan, like studying with others and sleeping properly, instead of expecting a tonic to do the work.

qa.q: What would have changed if Sahil had found his old timetable back then?
qa.a: He might have seen that stopping cricket, the study group and proper sleep were the likelier reasons, and not asked his aunt for more bottles.

grounding: It shows a teenager crediting a tonic for good marks when his own changed habits could explain them.

passage:
Himani twisted her ankle on the stairs eleven days before sports day, and the relay team had no reserve runner. The doctor at the clinic told her to rest it and to come back if it kept hurting or worried her. Himani did, lying on the sofa with her foot on two cushions. She also downloaded a free "healing sounds" app and played its humming every night, eyes closed, imagining the ankle mending.
By the second week the swelling had gone and she could jog around the terrace. "It's the app," she told Pallavi on the phone. "Healing sounds. I'm telling the whole team."
"You also rested like the doctor said," Pallavi replied. "Wouldn't it have healed anyway?"
Himani looked at her phone, the app still humming. "Maybe. But it healed faster than I thought."
"Faster than you thought isn't faster than it would have."

qa.q: What did the doctor tell Himani?
qa.a: To rest it and to come back if it kept hurting or worried her.

qa.q: Why does Himani give the app the credit?
qa.a: Himani felt eager to believe she'd done something special to heal in time for the relay, and since she played the app every night before her ankle got better, it got the credit.

qa.q: What could Himani tell her team that is more accurate?
qa.a: That she rested as the doctor said and used an app she found relaxing, but she can't tell whether the app did anything.

qa.q: What is Pallavi pointing out with the last line?
qa.a: That healing sooner than Himani expected doesn't show the app sped it up, because the ankle might have healed just as fast without it.

grounding: It shows a teenager, racing against sports day, crediting an app for a recovery that rest would likely have brought anyway.

passage:
Madhav, fifteen, held his report card up in the auto on the way home from school in Nagpur. Second term: 81 percent. First term: 64.
"It's the focus app," he told Shankar. "I started it in October. Twenty-five minutes study, five minutes break, and the little tree grows. That's it. That's the whole secret."
Shankar looked out at the traffic. "October is also when you stopped going to your cousin's wedding every weekend. And when your family finished shifting house."
"Yeah, but the app is what changed my brain."
"First term you were new in the school too."
"Everyone's new sometime." Madhav was already showing the auto driver the little tree on his phone. "I'm telling my whole tuition batch to download it."
Shankar shrugged and let it go.

qa.q: What was Madhav's first-term percentage?
qa.a: First term: 64.

qa.q: Why does Madhav feel so certain the app raised his marks?
qa.a: He started the app in October and the marks went up after, so the timing feels like proof, and he brushes aside the wedding weekends, the house shift and being new.

qa.q: What could Madhav check before telling his whole tuition batch?
qa.a: He could ask whether his marks would have risen anyway once the move, the weddings and being new were over, and see if others who use the app improve too.

qa.q: How does Shankar see Madhav's 'whole secret'?
qa.a: Shankar thinks the settled home and free weekends explain the jump, and seems tired of arguing when Madhav won't listen.

grounding: It shows a teenager crediting an app for scoring well when his results may simply have improved as his life settled down.

Sarita laughed. "Fine. Keep the thread. But we're still revising tonight."

qa.a: She lets him keep the thread but insists on revising; that keeps the real help going without turning the thread into a fight.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel when Vijay says she just wants credit?
qa.a: Sarita may feel a little hurt that her nights of explaining circuits are brushed aside, though she laughs it off.

passage: The week before the prelims, Nirmala bought a red-and-black thread from a stall at the Kolhar fair. She tied it on her wrist and then scored eighty-one in science, her best ever. "It's the thread," she told Vidya on the bus home, tapping it. "I'm never taking it off." Vidya glanced at her friend's notebook, crowded with diagrams. "You also studied every evening at my house for a month. You never did that before." "Lots of people study. Not everyone has this." Vidya didn't argue. In the next test Nirmala wore the thread but skipped the evening sessions for a cousin's wedding. She got fifty-four. Staring at the paper, she turned the thread round and round on her wrist, and slowly said, "Maybe it was the evenings."

qa.q: What score did Nirmala get in science after tying on the thread?
qa.a: She scored eighty-one in science, her best ever.

qa.q: Why did the thread feel responsible for the good mark to Nirmala?
qa.a: Nirmala felt proud and lucky, and the thread arrived just before her best mark, so it seemed to be the cause, while the month of studying felt ordinary.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do to keep her marks up next time?
qa.a: Keep the evening study sessions going, thread or no thread, since the fifty-four came when those sessions stopped.

qa.q: Why might Vidya have chosen not to argue on the bus?
qa.a: Vidya may have sensed that Nirmala was happy and attached to the thread, and that arguing would only make the thread seem more important.

grounding: Shows a teenager crediting a lucky thread for a high score when a month of study came with it.

passage: In the school hostel at Panchgani, Raghav caught a bad cold in the second week of term. On day four, his roommate gave him a bottle of herbal tonic from home. "My mother swears by it." Raghav drank it that night. By day seven, his cold was gone. He told everyone the tonic had cured him, and he wrote to his parents asking for three more bottles. Ganga didi, the hostel nurse, heard him in the corridor. "Raghav, how long do colds usually last?" He shrugged. "About a week?" "And yours lasted?" "...About a week." "What would have happened if you hadn't drunk the tonic?" He thought. "Maybe the same." "Maybe," she said. "Drink water, rest, and come to me if it gets worse or keeps going. And don't spend your money on bottles."

qa.q: When did Raghav's cold go away?
qa.a: By day seven, his cold was gone.

qa.q: Why did Raghav believe the tonic cured him?
qa.a: He felt relieved and grateful, and since he got better after drinking it, the tonic seemed to be the reason.

qa.q: What question from Ganga didi helped, and what advice did she give?
qa.a: She asked what would have happened without the tonic, since colds last about a week; she advised rest, water, and coming to her if it got worse or kept going.

qa.q: How might Raghav's roommate see the tonic now?
qa.a: The roommate may still trust it because of family, but might also wonder if colds just get better on their own.

grounding: Shows a teenager crediting a herbal tonic for curing his cold, when it would probably have cleared by itself.
